question: Give the complete identity profile of Project Tiger — type, launch year, administering body, parent ministry, original and current number of reserves, and latest addition.
cardAnswer: Project Tiger is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (NOT a statutory authority) launched in 1973. It is administered by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) under the Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change (MoEFCC). It started with 9 tiger reserves and currently has 56, with Guru Ghasidas-Tamor Pingla being the latest addition. The distinction between Project Tiger (the scheme) and NTCA (the statutory body created under WPA 1972 Amendment, 2006) is a classic conflation trap.

question: Describe the complete structure of a Tiger Reserve — the two zones, their definitions, how their boundaries are determined, and what legal protections apply.
cardAnswer: A Tiger Reserve has two zones. The Core (Critical Tiger Habitat) is established on scientific/objective criteria, kept inviolate, notified by the State Government with an Expert Committee — but critically, its inviolate status does NOT extinguish the rights of Scheduled Tribes and other forest dwellers; WPA explicitly protects those rights. The Buffer Zone is the peripheral area around the core that promotes co-existence of wildlife and human activity with lesser habitat protection; its boundaries are determined in consultation with the Gram Sabha and an Expert Committee. Buffer zone boundary changes require NTCA approval and cannot be altered unilaterally by the state.

question: What are all the powers and functions of the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)? Include its nature, parent legislation, and ministry.
cardAnswer: NTCA is a statutory authority established under the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2006, under MoEFCC. Its functions are: (1) Approve Tiger Conservation Plans made by State Governments (states make the plans; NTCA only approves). (2) Evaluate and assess sustainable ecology; prohibit ecologically unsustainable land use such as mining and industry in tiger reserves. (3) Establish standards and norms for tiger tourism in both core and buffer zones. (4) Gather data for conservation — disease surveillance, mortality surveys, patrolling reports. (5) Approve use of tiger reserves or connecting areas for non-tiger purposes in public interest, but this requires NBWL approval — not NTCA alone. (6) Extend tiger reserve management to adjacent areas through eco-development. (7) Capacity building for tiger reserve officers and staff.

question: Describe the complete methodology of the All India Tiger Estimation (AITE) — frequency, conducting bodies, all four phases with tools used, and the status of each technique.
cardAnswer: AITE is conducted every 4 years since 2006, jointly by NTCA and WII (Wildlife Institute of India) with state forest departments. The four phases are: Phase I — M-STrIPES App (Monitoring System for Tigers - Intensive Protection and Ecological Status): field data on signs, sightings, and human impact collected digitally; mandatory and primary for ground evidence. Phase II — Remote Sensing & GIS: habitat characterisation, vegetation indices, and land-use changes analysed via satellite imagery. Phase III — Camera Trapping & SECR: individual tigers identified by unique stripe patterns using ExtractCompare software; Spatially Explicit Capture-Recapture (SECR) models estimate population density; this is the gold standard for population figures. Phase IV — Intensive Annual Monitoring at tiger reserve level to track survival and recruitment between 4-year national cycles, using 25 cameras per 100 sq km and distance sampling for prey. DNA profiling of scat/hair is a supplementary/verification method, especially in low-density or high-canopy areas like Northeast India. Pugmark Census is now obsolete for counting — used only as a presence/absence index; population numbers are never derived from pugmarks.

question: What are all of India's bilateral and multilateral tiger conservation agreements? Include the type of agreement and specific focus for each partner.
cardAnswer: India has four bilateral agreements: (1) Nepal — MoU on controlling trans-border illegal trade and habitat connectivity; active and critical for the Terai Arc Landscape. (3) Russia — MoU on conservation genetics and disease dynamics; focused on Amur tiger research and cold-climate adaptations. question: Give the complete identity profile of Project Elephant — type, launch date, administering body, elephant's legal status, current population, global proportion, three core objectives, and nature of financial assistance.
cardAnswer: Project Elephant is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme launched in February 1992 (not 1973 — it came nearly 20 years after Project Tiger) under MoEFCC. It provides financial and technical assistance to states — it is not a direct implementation scheme. The elephant is India's National Heritage Animal (declared 2010). India's current national elephant population is 22,446 (All-India Synchronized Elephant Estimation, 2025), and India harbours more than 60% of the global Asian Elephant population. The three core objectives are: (1) Protect elephants, their habitat and corridors; (2) Address human-elephant conflict; (3) Welfare of domesticated elephants — this third objective is counterintuitive and frequently tested.

question: Describe all the specific tools and programmes used under Project Elephant for welfare, human-elephant conflict mitigation, and habitat policy — Gaja Suchana, Project RE-HAB, Gajraj, and RAPs.
cardAnswer: For domesticated elephant welfare: the Gaja Suchana App is used for mandatory DNA profiling of all captive elephants to prevent illegal trade and monitor welfare. For human-elephant conflict (HEC): Project RE-HAB (Reducing Elephant-Human Attacks using Bees) uses bee fences to deter elephants from human settlements. The Gajraj system is an AI-based intrusion detection system installed by Indian Railways to prevent elephant-train collisions on critical railway stretches. For habitat policy: Regional Action Plans (RAPs) represent a shift from state-specific to regional frameworks to account for transboundary elephant movement.

question: Describe the MIKE Programme completely — full name, initiation, authority, sub-regional office, all 10 Indian sites, and all three objectives including the PIKE Index.
cardAnswer: MIKE stands for Monitoring of Illegal Killings of Elephants. It was initiated in South Asia in 2003 as a result of a COP resolution of CITES — not IUCN or WWF. The Sub-Regional Support Office for South Asia is in New Delhi (supported by IUCN South Asia). There are 10 official MIKE sites in India: Chirang-Ripu, Dihing Patkai, Deomali, Garo Hills, Eastern Dooars, Mayurbhanj, Shivalik, Mysore, Nilgiri, and Wayanad. Note: there are 33 Elephant Reserves but only 10 MIKE sites — the numbers differ significantly. The three objectives are: (1) Measure levels and trends in illegal elephant hunting; (2) Identify causes of changes in those trends; (3) Evaluate the impact of CITES decisions on illegal killing trends. MIKE calculates the PIKE Index (Proportion of Illegally Killed Elephants) to monitor poaching pressure.
